title: Isostasy — Airy and Pratt Models
ordering_justification: Isostasy logically follows the study of Earth's layered internal structure (topics 7-8) and plate tectonics (topics 9-12). Having understood that the crust sits atop a denser mantle, students are ready to grasp the hydrostatic principle by which crustal blocks of varying density and thickness 'float' in gravitational equilibrium on the asthenosphere. This topic is the mechanical bridge between static crustal structure and dynamic processes: it explains why the Himalayas have deep roots exceeding 70 km, why the Indo-Gangetic Plain is a crustal depression (foreland basin), why Scandinavia is still rising centuries after glacial melting (post-glacial rebound), and how erosion and uplift form a feedback loop governing mountain longevity. Isostasy also connects to gravity anomalies measured by GRACE satellites, crustal thickness mapping by ISRO, and sea-level correction methodologies — all recurring UPSC current-affairs hooks.
concept_checklist: Isostasy is the state of gravitational equilibrium in which segments of Earth's lithosphere 'float' on the denser, plastic asthenosphere at a level determined by their thickness and density, analogous to icebergs floating in water.

The Airy model (G.B. Airy, 1855) proposes that crustal blocks of uniform density but varying thickness achieve isostatic balance through differences in the depth of their root: mountains have deep roots extending into the mantle, while plains have shallow roots — the crust acts like floating columns of equal density but different height.

The Pratt model (J.H. Pratt, 1855) proposes that crustal columns all reach the same depth of compensation but have varying densities: mountains correspond to less dense material, ocean floors to denser material — compensation is achieved horizontally across columns of different density.

The compensation depth (isostatic compensation depth) is the level below which pressure is equal in all vertical columns; above this depth, density variations in the crust produce the observed topography; below it, pressure is hydrostatically balanced.

The Himalayas have crustal roots extending more than 70 km below the surface — far greater than the average continental crustal thickness of 35 km — consistent with Airy's model of thickened crust under high topography.

The Indo-Gangetic Plain is a foreland basin formed because the immense weight of the Himalayan orogen depresses the Indian Plate lithosphere ahead of the collision zone, creating a flexural moat that is subsequently filled with Himalayan-derived sediments — an expression of flexural isostasy.

Post-glacial rebound (isostatic uplift) occurs when the mass of an ice sheet is removed after glaciation; the lithosphere, previously depressed by ice load, slowly recovers its isostatic equilibrium — Scandinavia is rising at ~1 cm/year and has rebounded ~300 m since the last glacial maximum.

Gravity anomalies reveal isostatic state: a positive Bouguer anomaly (measured gravity exceeds predicted) typically indicates a mass excess or thin crust (e.g., ocean floors, rift zones); a negative Bouguer anomaly indicates a mass deficit or deep crustal root (e.g., the Himalayas), confirming isostatic compensation.

Vening Meinesz proposed a regional flexural isostasy model (elastic plate model) to reconcile the fact that compensation is not always purely local: the lithosphere has rigidity and bends as a plate rather than responding as isolated columns — this explains the width of foreland basins and oceanic trenches.

Isostasy and erosion create a feedback loop: as mountains erode (mass removed), the crust rebounds isostatically (uplift), exposing deeper crustal rocks; this cycling explains why ancient cratons have exhumed deep metamorphic terrains even though they are topographically low today.

content_sections.title: Foundation Understanding — How the Crust Floats

blocks.title: Start Here
blocks.text: Why doesn't the Himalaya sink into the Earth under its own immense weight? Why is the ground beneath Scandinavia still quietly rising — centuries after the last Ice Age ended? The answer is isostasy: the Earth's crust 'floats' on the mantle just as an iceberg floats on ocean water. The higher the mountain, the deeper its root. The heavier the glacier, the more the crust sags. Remove the load, and the crust bounces back. This single principle — crustal buoyancy — underpins mountain building, ocean basin formation, post-glacial landscapes, and gravity measurements from space.

items.label: Year both Airy & Pratt models proposed

blocks.text: What Is Isostasy?

**Isostasy** (from Greek: isos = equal, stasis = standing) is the state of **gravitational equilibrium** in which the Earth's lithosphere 'floats' on the denser, viscous **asthenosphere**, much like wood floating in water. Each column of rock, from the surface down to a fixed **compensation depth**, must exert the same pressure at that depth. Where crust is thick or low-density (mountains, continents), it floats higher and has a deeper root. Where crust is thin or high-density (ocean floors, rifts), it sits lower. The **Himalayas** — towering 8 km above sea level — exist only because their crust extends more than **70 km deep** into the mantle, providing the buoyancy needed to support that height.

Think of an iceberg: the taller the visible part above water, the deeper the submerged root below. A mountain range is Earth's iceberg — for every kilometre above the surface, there is a proportionally deeper root below. A plain has little root; a deep ocean floor has the least. Remove the mountain by erosion, and just as a melting iceberg bobs upward, the crust rebounds — this is post-glacial (isostatic) uplift.

The concept of isostasy was first articulated in **1855** — almost simultaneously — by two British scientists approaching the problem from different angles. **George Biddell Airy** was Astronomer Royal, and **John Henry Pratt** was a mathematician and Archdeacon of Calcutta. Both were trying to explain a puzzling anomaly in the **Great Trigonometrical Survey of India**: why did the plumb bob near the **Himalayas** deflect less than expected toward the mountain mass? The answer, they independently concluded, was that the mountains were compensated at depth — there was less dense material below the mountains than under the plains, reducing the net gravitational pull. Their contrasting explanations of how this compensation worked became the two foundational models of isostasy.

The **Indo-Gangetic Plain** is itself a consequence of isostasy. As the Indian Plate collides with Eurasia and the Himalayas rise, the enormous weight of the mountain belt depresses the Indian Plate ahead of it, forming a **foreland basin** — a long, shallow trough that fills with Himalayan sediments washed down by rivers. The Ganga, Yamuna, Brahmaputra and their tributaries are filling this isostatic depression, building the most fertile floodplain in the world. The plain is not flat because rivers deposited sediment; it is flat because isostatic depression and sediment infill are in dynamic equilibrium.
The Two Models — Airy vs Pratt

left.label: Airy Model (1855)
items: All crustal columns have the SAME density
Mountains float higher because they have DEEPER ROOTS extending into mantle
Root thickness proportional to surface height
Like icebergs: same material, different sizes
Favoured for: continental mountain belts (Himalayas, Alps, Andes)

right.label: Pratt Model (1855)
items: All crustal columns reach the SAME depth of compensation
Mountains are elevated because they are made of LOWER DENSITY material
Higher column = less dense; lower column = more dense
Like floating blocks of different materials (wood vs steel)
Favoured for: ocean ridges, volcanic plateaux with different rock types

blocks.text: Key Terms

terms.definition: State of gravitational equilibrium where crustal blocks 'float' on the denser mantle asthenosphere. Each crustal column exerts equal pressure at the **compensation depth**.
The depth below which pressure is equal in all adjacent vertical columns. Above it, density/thickness differences exist; below it, pressure is hydrostatically equal. Typically ~100-120 km.
Isostasy achieved by **varying crustal thickness** (root depth) at constant density. Mountains have deep roots; plains have shallow roots.
Isostasy achieved by **varying crustal density** at constant compensation depth. Mountains = low-density crust; ocean floors = high-density crust.
Slow rise of land after removal of glacial ice load, as crust returns to isostatic equilibrium. Scandinavia rising ~1 cm/yr; total rebound since LGM ~300 m.
Equipotential surface of Earth's gravity field corresponding to mean sea level. Deviations from geoid (geoid undulations) reflect internal mass distributions and isostatic anomalies.
Pressure at any depth due to the weight of overlying rock column. Isostasy requires equal lithostatic pressure at the compensation depth across all adjacent columns.
A crustal depression formed by **flexural isostasy** in front of a mountain belt; the Indian-Gangetic Plain is the classic example, formed by Himalayan loading of the Indian Plate.

blocks.text: NCERT Key Points — Isostasy

blocks.title: Core NCERT Concepts on Isostasy
items: **Isostasy** maintains that the lithosphere is in gravitational equilibrium, floating on the plastic asthenosphere.
**Airy hypothesis**: mountains have deep roots; plains have shallow roots; same density throughout the crust.
**Pratt hypothesis**: all crustal columns reach the same compensation depth; high ground = less dense material.
**Evidence from India**: the Great Trigonometrical Survey plumb-bob anomaly near the Himalayas was the original motivation for both models.
**Post-glacial rebound** is the most direct observable evidence that isostatic adjustment is an ongoing, measurable process.
**Erosion-isostasy feedback**: as mountains are eroded, crust rebounds isostatically, explaining why ancient mountain roots are preserved deep in cratons.
NCERT emphasises that **neither model alone explains all observations** — Vening Meinesz's regional/flexural model better accounts for the width of compensation zones.

content_sections.title: Advanced Analysis — Flexural Isostasy, Gravity Anomalies, and Indian Context

blocks.text: Vening Meinesz and Flexural (Regional) Isostasy

Both Airy and Pratt models assume **local isostasy** — each crustal column independently achieves equilibrium. Dutch geophysicist **Felix Andries Vening Meinesz** (1930s) demonstrated from submarine gravity measurements that compensation is often **regional**: the lithosphere has significant **elastic rigidity** and bends as a continuous plate rather than responding as isolated columns. Under a surface load (mountain, ice sheet, volcanic island), the lithosphere flexes downward across a zone much **wider** than the load itself — creating a peripheral **forebulge** beyond the depression zone. This **flexural isostasy** model (elastic plate model) better explains: (1) the width of the Indo-Gangetic foreland basin (400-500 km wide, yet Himalayan load is concentrated), (2) oceanic trenches adjacent to subducting slabs, (3) the broad peripheral raised rims (forebulges) seen around sedimentary basins.
Gravity Anomalies and Isostatic State

**Gravity anomalies** are the difference between observed gravity and theoretically predicted gravity for a given latitude and elevation. **Bouguer anomaly** (corrects for topography and elevation) is the standard measure of isostatic state: A **positive Bouguer anomaly** means observed gravity exceeds the theoretical value — indicating a local **mass excess** relative to surroundings, implying thin crust or high-density material at depth. This is typical of **ocean floors** (thin, dense oceanic crust) and **rift valleys** (thinned crust). A **negative Bouguer anomaly** means observed gravity is less than predicted — indicating a local **mass deficit**, implying a deep, low-density crustal root beneath the surface. The **Himalayas** exhibit strongly negative Bouguer anomalies (as low as −500 mGal), confirming deep crustal roots >70 km — exactly as Airy's model predicts. **Isostatically compensated** regions (in perfect isostatic balance) show near-zero **isostatic anomaly** (a refined correction beyond Bouguer). Persistent non-zero isostatic anomalies reveal regions that are NOT in equilibrium — actively rising or sinking.
Post-Glacial Rebound — Scandinavia and Antarctica

The most dramatic modern example of isostasy in action is **post-glacial rebound** (also called **glacio-isostatic adjustment, GIA**). During the last glacial maximum (~20,000 years ago), the Fennoscandian ice sheet (up to 3 km thick) depressed the lithosphere beneath Scandinavia by up to **800 m**. As the ice melted (~10,000 BCE), the crustal depression began to recover. Scandinavia is still rising at **~1 cm/year** at its centre (Gulf of Bothnia), and has rebounded approximately **300 m** since deglaciation — with another 100-200 m of rebound expected before it reaches equilibrium. **Antarctica** and **Greenland** are undergoing the same process beneath their present ice sheets: the crust below Antarctica is currently depressed by up to **2 km** by the ice load. Were the Antarctic ice sheet to melt, land currently below sea level in West Antarctica would eventually rebound above sea level — a process taking **10,000-100,000 years** given the asthenosphere's high viscosity.
India — Himalayan Deep Roots and the Indo-Gangetic Basin

India provides two textbook isostasy examples. First, the **Himalayas**: geodetic and seismic studies show that the Indian crust thickens from ~35 km under the plains to **>70 km** under the High Himalayas — the deepest continental crustal root on Earth. This massive root provides the buoyancy to support peaks like Everest (8,849 m). The crust is still thickening as the India-Eurasia collision continues at ~5 cm/year. Second, the **Indo-Gangetic Plain**: as the Indian Plate underthrusts Eurasia, the leading edge of the Indian lithosphere is **flexurally depressed** forming the Himalayan foreland basin. This 2,400-km-long trough, filled with up to **5 km of Quaternary alluvial sediments**, is a direct consequence of Vening Meinesz-style flexural loading. The subsidence rate of the basin matches predicted values from elastic plate models of the Indian lithosphere's rigidity.
Isostasy and the Erosion-Uplift Feedback

A crucial UPSC-relevant insight: mountains do not simply erode down and disappear. As erosion removes mass from peaks, the crustal load decreases, and **isostatic rebound** raises the remaining crust. This creates a self-sustaining cycle: **erosion → mass reduction → isostatic uplift → continued erosion at higher elevations → deeper crustal rocks exposed**. For every 1 km eroded off a mountain, ~0.8 km of isostatic uplift occurs. This means the **total erosion** required to reduce a mountain belt to sea level is 5-7 times the original height. The **Aravallis** (one of the world's oldest fold mountains, ~2.5 billion years) are now mere low hills (~900 m), yet their metamorphic rocks were once 25-30 km deep — all exhumed through this erosion-isostasy cycling over billions of years. Modern Himalayan rivers export ~1 billion tonnes of sediment per year, yet the Himalayas continue to rise — because isostatic rebound outpaces erosion.

blocks.title: Advanced: Geoid Undulations and Isostasy
blocks.content: The geoid (the equipotential surface matching mean sea level) is not a perfect ellipsoid — it has undulations (bumps and hollows) up to ±100 m caused by internal mass variations. Isostatic compensation directly shapes the geoid: mountain roots (mass deficit) pull the geoid downward locally; high-density oceanic crust pulls it upward. The Indian Ocean geoid low (a depression of ~100 m centered southwest of India) is partly attributed to a cold, dense subducted slab remnant in the lower mantle beneath. GRACE satellite data has mapped these geoid undulations at 300 km resolution globally — detecting ice mass loss, groundwater depletion, and post-glacial rebound simultaneously. The Indian Ocean geoid low remains one of the largest unexplained geoid features on Earth, and isostatic adjustment is one of the competing hypotheses.

blocks.text: Recent Developments (2023-2026)

blocks.title: GPS Measurement of Post-Glacial Rebound (Scandinavia & Antarctica)
blocks.text: Continuous GPS networks in Scandinavia (BIFROST project) and Antarctica (POLENET) now measure **glacio-isostatic adjustment (GIA)** in real time with millimetre accuracy. Scandinavia's uplift rate of **~1 cm/year** at the Gulf of Bothnia is one of the best-quantified isostatic signals on Earth. In Antarctica, GPS stations beneath ice detect crustal response to ongoing ice mass loss from the West Antarctic Ice Sheet — uplift rates of up to **4 cm/year** have been measured in the Antarctic Peninsula (faster than expected, indicating a less viscous mantle). These measurements are critical for **correcting sea-level rise estimates**: raw tide gauge data must subtract the local land-level change (GIA component) to obtain the true ocean volume change. UPSC may frame this as: 'Why might tide gauges overestimate sea-level rise in some regions and underestimate it in others?'

blocks.title: GRACE Satellite Gravity Anomaly Mapping — India Focus
blocks.text: The **GRACE** (Gravity Recovery and Climate Experiment) and its successor **GRACE-FO** satellites (NASA/DLR) measure Earth's gravity field monthly by tracking the distance between two co-orbiting satellites. Changes in this distance reveal mass redistribution beneath the surface. For India, GRACE data has shown: (1) **Himalayan crustal root** dynamics — the negative gravity anomaly over the Himalayas is one of the strongest on Earth, confirming >70 km crustal roots; (2) **Indo-Gangetic Plain groundwater depletion** — GRACE detected massive groundwater loss (~54 km³/year in the Indo-Gangetic Aquifer, 2002-2016), detected as a positive gravity anomaly change; (3) **Post-monsoon recharge signals** across the Deccan and peninsular India. ISRO's **NavIC** geodetic network complements GRACE by providing surface positioning, enabling isostatic uplift detection at centimetre scale across India.

blocks.title: Isostatic Rebound and Sea-Level Measurement Complexity
blocks.text: A major contemporary scientific debate concerns **relative vs absolute sea-level rise**. Absolute sea-level rise (ocean volume expansion + ice melt water input) is ~3.6 mm/year globally. However, what people experience is **relative sea-level change** = absolute rise ± vertical land movement. In post-glacially rebounding regions (Scandinavia, northern Canada), land rises faster than sea level, so relative sea level is **falling** despite global warming. In regions where crust is subsiding (Jakarta, Bangladesh delta, US Gulf Coast), relative sea level rises faster than the global average. Properly correcting tide gauge and satellite altimetry records for **GIA (isostatic component)** requires global models of mantle viscosity — a major source of uncertainty in IPCC sea-level projections.

blocks.title: ISRO Geodesy and Crustal Movement Surveys in India
blocks.text: India's **National Centre for Earth Science Studies (NCESS)** and **ISRO's Space Applications Centre** operate continuous GPS/GNSS networks that detect millimetre-level crustal movements across the Indian subcontinent. Results confirm: (1) The Indian Plate is moving **~5 cm/year** northward into Eurasia; (2) The Himalayas are rising by **~5 mm/year** (net, after erosion); (3) The Kutch region (Gujarat) shows residual crustal stress from the 2001 Bhuj earthquake; (4) Subsidence of ~5-10 mm/year in parts of the Ganga delta from sediment compaction and groundwater extraction (not isostatic). These surveys distinguish tectonic motion from isostatic adjustment — both affect land elevation but have different timescales and spatial patterns.

blocks.title: Reservoir-Induced Seismicity and Local Isostatic Loading
blocks.text: Large dams impound water that adds a significant **surface mass load** on the crust — an artificial isostatic perturbation. The weight of reservoir water can flex the crust downward by centimetres and increase pore-water pressure in faults, potentially triggering earthquakes (**reservoir-induced seismicity**). India's **Koyna Dam** (Maharashtra) is one of the world's most studied cases: the Koyna–Warna reservoir has triggered thousands of earthquakes since 1962, including the devastating **M6.3 Koyna earthquake (1967)**. The Ministry of Earth Sciences' proposed **Koyna deep drilling project** aims to study this phenomenon — drilling into active fault zones to directly measure stress and fluid pressure changes. Understanding isostatic loading from reservoir impoundment is directly relevant to dam safety assessment and EIA requirements for large infrastructure projects in seismically active regions.
Common Misconceptions UPSC Tests

blocks.wrong: In the Airy model, higher mountains have lower-density rock compared to plains (i.e., confusing Airy with Pratt)
blocks.correct: In the AIRY model, all crustal rocks have the SAME density — height differences are compensated by ROOT DEPTH differences (deeper root under mountains). It is the PRATT model that uses density variation. This Airy-vs-Pratt confusion is the single most common UPSC mistake on isostasy.

blocks.wrong: In the Pratt model, mountains have deeper roots into the mantle
blocks.correct: In the PRATT model, ALL crustal columns reach the SAME compensation depth — there are NO differential roots. Instead, mountain columns are made of LESS DENSE material (lower density = same depth, but still floats higher). Deep roots are exclusively the Airy model concept.

blocks.wrong: A positive Bouguer gravity anomaly over a mountain range indicates thick crust and deep roots
blocks.correct: A NEGATIVE Bouguer anomaly indicates thick crust / deep roots (mass deficit due to low-density root). A POSITIVE Bouguer anomaly indicates thin crust / mass excess. The Himalayas have strongly NEGATIVE Bouguer anomalies (~−500 mGal). Positive anomalies are typical of ocean basins and rift zones (thin, dense crust).

blocks.wrong: Post-glacial rebound means sea level falls after an ice age ends because water is released onto the land
blocks.correct: Post-glacial rebound refers to the CRUSTAL UPLIFT (land rising) after the ice load is removed — it is an isostatic process, not a sea-level process. Sea level actually RISES after ice melts (more water in oceans). In rebounding regions like Scandinavia, RELATIVE sea level falls because the land rises faster than the sea, but ABSOLUTE sea level rises globally.

blocks.wrong: The Indo-Gangetic Plain is flat because rivers deposited alluvium on a pre-existing flat surface
blocks.correct: The Indo-Gangetic Plain is a FORELAND BASIN created by FLEXURAL ISOSTASY — the weight of the Himalayas depresses the Indian Plate ahead of the collision zone, forming a crustal trough. Rivers subsequently fill this isostatically-created depression with sediments. The plain's flatness is a consequence of isostatic subsidence + sediment infill, not a primary surface.

blocks.wrong: Isostasy guarantees that the crust is always in perfect isostatic equilibrium
blocks.correct: Isostasy is the TENDENCY toward equilibrium, not a state of permanent equilibrium. Actively rising mountain belts, regions undergoing glaciation/deglaciation, subsiding sedimentary basins, and regions above subducting slabs are all in ISOSTATIC DISEQUILIBRIUM — the crust adjusts toward equilibrium over geological time (thousands to millions of years, depending on mantle viscosity).

blocks.wrong: Vening Meinesz's model is simply a combination of Airy and Pratt models
blocks.correct: Vening Meinesz proposed a fundamentally DIFFERENT mechanism: REGIONAL (FLEXURAL) isostasy. He argued that the lithosphere has ELASTIC RIGIDITY and bends as a plate, distributing the load laterally. This is neither Airy (local density compensation) nor Pratt (local density variation) — it explains features like the WIDTH of foreland basins and forebulges that neither local model can account for.

blocks.text: AIRY = All same density, varies Root depth (A = Analogous to icebergs — same ice, different size) | PRATT = same comPensation depth, varies densiTy (P = Plates of different materials — wood vs metal) | Mnemonic: 'AIRY heights come from DEEP roots; PRATT heights come from LIGHT rocks' | POST-GLACIAL REBOUND = Remove Ice, Rise Up (RIRU) | BOUGUER: Mountains = MINUS (negative); Oceans = PLUS (positive)

pyqs.question_text:
Consider the following statements:
1. Isostasy is the condition of gravitational equilibrium between the Earth's lithosphere and asthenosphere.
2. According to Airy's hypothesis, higher mountains are composed of less dense crustal material compared to the surrounding plains.
3. The Himalayas exhibit negative Bouguer gravity anomalies, indicating the presence of deep crustal roots.
Which of the above statements is/are correct?
pyqs.explanation: Statement 1 is correct — isostasy is precisely this gravitational equilibrium. Statement 2 is WRONG — it describes the PRATT model, not the Airy model. In the Airy model, density is constant but root depth varies (deeper under higher mountains). Statement 3 is correct — the Himalayas have strongly negative Bouguer anomalies (up to −500 mGal), confirming crustal roots exceeding 70 km depth.

pyqs.question_text: Which of the following best explains the phenomenon of 'post-glacial rebound' observed in Scandinavia?
pyqs.answer_text: As the weight of the Pleistocene ice sheet was removed after melting, the lithosphere, previously depressed by glacial loading, slowly rose back toward isostatic equilibrium.
pyqs.explanation: Post-glacial rebound is a direct consequence of isostasy. The Fennoscandian ice sheet (up to 3 km thick) depressed the crust by ~800 m. After deglaciation (~10,000 BCE), the crust began recovering; Scandinavia is still rising at ~1 cm/year. This is NEITHER a tectonic nor volcanic phenomenon — it is purely isostatic, driven by the viscoelastic response of the asthenosphere to load removal.

pyqs.question_text: Distinguish between the Airy and Pratt models of isostasy. How does the concept of isostasy explain the origin of the Indo-Gangetic Plain and the deep roots of the Himalayas?
pyqs.answer_text: Airy model (1855): assumes uniform crustal density; isostatic equilibrium achieved by variation in crustal thickness — mountains have deep roots, plains have shallow roots. Analogous to icebergs of the same material but different sizes. Pratt model (1855): assumes uniform compensation depth; equilibrium achieved by lateral density variation — mountains have low-density crust, ocean floors have high-density crust. Indo-Gangetic Plain: Flexural isostasy (Vening Meinesz model) — the enormous weight of the Himalayan orogen flexes the Indian Plate downward, creating a foreland basin ~400-500 km wide, subsequently filled with 3-5 km of alluvial sediments from Himalayan rivers. Himalayan roots: Seismic refraction and gravity data confirm the Indian crust thickens from ~35 km under the plains to >70 km under the High Himalayas — the deepest continental root on Earth, consistent with Airy's model. The strongly negative Bouguer anomaly (up to −500 mGal) confirms this mass deficit at depth.
pyqs.explanation: Key Mains answer structure: define isostasy → distinguish Airy vs Pratt with mechanism and analogy → apply Airy to Himalayan deep roots (cite >70 km, negative Bouguer anomaly) → apply flexural isostasy to Indo-Gangetic foreland basin (cite Vening Meinesz, sediment fill) → conclude with ongoing nature: India-Eurasia collision still thickening the crust and depressing the basin.
